# Statistical Inference & Testing

### The Normal World, t-Tests, and Non-Parametric Alternatives

**Chapter 7 · From Data to Thesis**

Dr. Polla Fattah

---

## The Fundamental Leap of Research

Empirical science is almost always about **more people than we can measure**:

- A study of 600 students matters because of what it reveals about **all graduate students**.
- A clinical trial of 150 patients matters because of future patients who will receive the therapy.

> **Statistical inference is the mathematical discipline of generalizing from the sample we measured to the population we care about—while rigorously quantifying uncertainty.**

A second sample would give slightly different numbers; a third another. How do we decide when a sample difference is real?

---

## What We Will Master Today

By the end of this lecture deck, you will be able to:

- Distinguish population **parameters** ($\mu, \sigma$) from sample **statistics** ($\bar{x}, s$).
- Demonstrate the **Central Limit Theorem (CLT)** and the behavior of the **Standard Error**.
- Calculate, plot, and interpret parametric and **bootstrap confidence intervals**.
- Demystify the **p-value** through computer simulation (**permutation test**).
- Quantify the trade-offs between **Type I errors**, **Type II errors**, and **statistical power**.
- Avoid the **multiple testing crisis** ($1 - 0.95^k$).
- Conduct and interpret **one-sample**, **two-sample (Welch)**, and **paired t-tests**.
- Calculate and contextualize standardized effect sizes (**Cohen's d**).
- Deploy **non-parametric tests** (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank) and **Chi-Square ($\chi^2$) tests**.
- Write publication-standard **APA results sections**.

---

# Sampling Distributions & The Central Limit Theorem

### The Engine of Inferential Statistics

---

## Parameters vs. Statistics

```
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| POPULATION (All Graduate Students)                            |
| Fixed, unobservable truth. Summarized by PARAMETERS:          |
|   - True mean sleep:       μ (mu)                             |
|   - True standard dev:     σ (sigma)                          |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
                               |
                               | Random Sample (N = 600)
                               v
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| SAMPLE (Elaf's Measured Cohort)                               |
| Observable, fluctuating reality. Summarized by STATISTICS:    |
|   - Sample mean sleep:     x̄ = 6.38 hours                     |
|   - Sample standard dev:   s = 1.02 hours                     |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

## Simulating the Sampling Distribution in R

Treat the 600 students as a known population and draw 1,000 samples of size 5 and size 30 from the skewed caffeine variable:

```r
library(data2thesis)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

first_sem <- semesters |>
  filter(semester == 1) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id))

caffeine_pop <- na.omit(first_sem$caffeine_mg)

set.seed(2026)
means_5  <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(caffeine_pop, size = 5)))
means_30 <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(caffeine_pop, size = 30)))
```

---

## Visualizing the Central Limit Theorem

```r
sim_df <- tibble(
  mean_val = c(means_5, means_30),
  size     = rep(c("Samples of N = 5", "Samples of N = 30"), each = 1000)
)

ggplot(sim_df, aes(x = mean_val)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 35, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ size, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Sampling Distribution of the Mean", x = "Sample Mean Caffeine (mg)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

```
Samples of N = 5 (Wide, Skewed)      Samples of N = 30 (Narrow, Bell-shaped)
        +--+                                    +---+
       /    \____                              /     \
     -+----------\---                        -+-------+-
```

### Three Foundational Insights:
1. **Unbiasedness:** Both distributions center precisely on the true population mean (281 mg).
2. **Precision:** Samples of 30 cluster far more tightly than samples of 5.
3. **The Central Limit Theorem:** Even though individual caffeine values are severely skewed, sample means of $N \ge 30$ are **symmetrical and normally distributed**.

---

## The Standard Error of the Mean

The standard deviation of the sampling distribution is the **Standard Error (SE)**:

$$SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

Comparing simulation vs. theoretical formula:

```r
# Empirical standard deviation across 1,000 simulated sample means:
sd(means_30)
#> [1] 31.84

# Theoretical formula:
sd(caffeine_pop) / sqrt(30)
#> [1] 31.87
```

> **The Quadrupling Law of Research Design:** Because $n$ sits under a square root, **halving your standard error requires quadrupling your sample size.**

---

# Confidence Intervals

### Replacing Point Estimates with Plausible Ranges

---

## What is a Confidence Interval?

A point estimate ($\bar{x} = 6.38$ hrs) gives no indication of precision.

A **95% Confidence Interval** provides a range of values that are plausible for the true parameter $\mu$:

$$\text{Approximate 95% CI} = \bar{x} \pm 2 \times SE = \bar{x} \pm 1.96 \left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right)$$

```r
t.test(first_sem$sleep_hours)$conf.int
#> [1] 6.297464 6.462740
#> attr(,"conf.level")
#> [1] 0.95
```

We are 95% confident that the true average nocturnal sleep of graduate students lies between **6.30 and 6.46 hours**.

---

## Common Misconception: "Mean $\pm$ SE"

Many theses report: *"Sleep averaged $6.38 \pm 0.04$ hours."*

- Examiners often mistake this for a confidence interval.
- $SE$ represents only **half** the width of an approximate 68% interval ($\pm 1 SE$).
- A 95% interval requires approximately **$\pm 2 SE$**.

> **Thesis Rule:** Always report the explicit confidence interval:
> *"M = 6.38 hours, 95% CI [6.30, 6.46]."*

---

## Non-Parametric Bootstrap Confidence Intervals

What if we need a confidence interval for a statistic with no tidy formula (e.g., the **median**)?

The **Bootstrap Principle** (Efron, 1979): Resample the data *with replacement* thousands of times:

```r
set.seed(1)
small_sample <- sample(caffeine_pop, 40)

# Resample 2,000 medians with replacement:
boot_medians <- replicate(2000, {
  median(sample(small_sample, replace = TRUE))
})

# Percentile confidence interval:
quantile(boot_medians, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
#>  2.5% 97.5% 
#>   180   320 
```

The bootstrap requires zero distributional assumptions and works for medians, ratios, and correlation coefficients.

---

# The Logic of Hypothesis Testing

### Demystifying p-Values through Permutations

---

## Testing RQ3: The Wellbeing Workshop

Does attending the 6-week workshop improve graduate student wellbeing in Semester 2?

```r
semester2 <- semesters |>
  filter(semester == 2) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id))

observed_diff <- mean(semester2$wellbeing[semester2$workshop == "Invited"]) -
                 mean(semester2$wellbeing[semester2$workshop == "Not invited"])

observed_diff
#> [1] 5.21
```

Invited students scored **5.21 points higher**.

- Is 5.21 a real therapeutic improvement?
- Or is it merely random luck in who received an invitation?

---

## The Permutation Test: Building the Null Distribution

If the workshop does nothing ($H_0$), the labels "Invited" and "Not invited" are meaningless stickers.

We can shuffle the labels 5,000 times to see what differences pure chance creates:

```r
set.seed(2026)

null_differences <- replicate(5000, {
  shuffled_labels <- sample(semester2$workshop)
  mean(semester2$wellbeing[shuffled_labels == "Invited"]) -
  mean(semester2$wellbeing[shuffled_labels == "Not invited"])
})
```

---

## Visualizing the Permutation Test

```r
ggplot(data.frame(gap = null_differences), aes(x = gap)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = observed_diff, colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Permutation Test: 5,000 Random Shuffles of Workshop Labels",
    subtitle = "Red Line = Observed Difference (+5.21 points)",
    x = "Difference in Group Means Under H0", y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

```
               Null Distribution (Pure Chance)
                          +---+
                        /       \
                     --+---------+--               | Observed (+5.21)
                    -3     0    +3                 |
```

In 5,000 shuffles, pure chance never produced a difference of $+5.21$.

$$p = \frac{\text{Count}(\ge |5.21|)}{5000} = \frac{0}{5000} \rightarrow p < .001$$

---

## Contrast: Permutation on GPA by Gender

Testing an association where no difference is expected:

```r
gpa_diff <- mean(first_sem$gpa[first_sem$gender == "Female"], na.rm = TRUE) -
            mean(first_sem$gpa[first_sem$gender == "Male"], na.rm = TRUE)

gpa_null <- replicate(5000, {
  shuffled <- sample(first_sem$gender)
  mean(first_sem$gpa[shuffled == "Female"], na.rm = TRUE) -
  mean(first_sem$gpa[shuffled == "Male"], na.rm = TRUE)
})

c(Observed = gpa_diff, p_value = mean(abs(gpa_null) >= abs(gpa_diff)))
```

```
  Observed    p_value 
0.01242105 0.62880000 
```

A difference of $0.01$ GPA points is generated by pure chance in **63% of shuffles**. We retain $H_0$.

---

## What a p-Value Actually Means

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| WHAT A p-VALUE IS:                                          |
| The probability of obtaining data as extreme as (or more    |
| extreme than) what was observed, ASSUMING THAT H0 IS TRUE.  |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| WHAT A p-VALUE IS NOT:                                      |
| 1. NOT the probability that H0 is true.                     |
| 2. NOT the probability that your hypothesis H1 is true.     |
| 3. NOT the probability that the result happened by chance.  |
| 4. NOT a measure of the size or importance of an effect!    |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
```

---

# Decision Errors & Statistical Power

### False Alarms and Missed Discoveries

---

## Type I and Type II Errors

```
                                  TRUE REALITY IN POPULATION
                             H0 is True (No effect)   H1 is True (Real effect)
Decision: Reject H0          TYPE I ERROR (alpha)     CORRECT DECISION
                             (False Positive / Alarm) (Statistical Power = 1-beta)

Decision: Retain H0          CORRECT DECISION         TYPE II ERROR (beta)
                             (True Negative)          (False Negative / Miss)
```

- **$\alpha$ (Significance Level):** Typically set to $.05$. In 5% of tests where nothing happens, we get a false alarm.
- **$\beta$ (Miss Rate):** Typically targeted at $.20$.
- **Power ($1 - \beta$):** Probability of detecting a real effect (Target: $80\%$).

---

## Simulating the 5% False Alarm Rate

Splitting 600 students into two random groups 1,000 times on pure noise:

```r
set.seed(7)
false_alarms <- replicate(1000, {
  fake_group <- sample(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 300))
  t.test(first_sem$wellbeing ~ fake_group)$p.value < 0.05
})

mean(false_alarms)
#> [1] 0.048   <-- Exactly ~5% false alarms occur by chance!
```

---

## The Danger of Multiple Testing

What happens if you run 20 independent tests on variables where $H_0$ is true?

$$P(\text{At least 1 false alarm}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^k = 1 - (0.95)^{20} \approx 64.2\%$$

```r
set.seed(8)
multi_test_sim <- replicate(1000, {
  p_vals <- replicate(20, t.test(rnorm(30), rnorm(30))$p.value)
  any(p_vals < 0.05)
})

mean(multi_test_sim)
#> [1] 0.651
```

> **Warning:** A thesis that tests 20 uncorrected relationships has a **65% chance of finding a false "discovery"** that disappears upon replication.

---

# The t-Test Family

### One-Sample, Two-Sample, and Paired Comparisons

---

## One-Sample t-Test: Testing RQ2 (Sleep Threshold)

Do graduate students sleep less than the recommended 7.0 hours?

$$H_0: \mu = 7.0 \quad \text{vs.} \quad H_1: \mu \neq 7.0$$

$$t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}} = \frac{6.38 - 7.00}{1.02 / \sqrt{588}} = -14.77$$

```r
sleep_test <- t.test(first_sem$sleep_hours, mu = 7.0)
sleep_test
```

```
	One Sample t-test

data:  first_sem$sleep_hours
t = -14.768, df = 587, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 7
95 percent confidence interval:
 6.297464 6.462740
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 6.380102 
```

Students sleep an average of $6.38$ hours—statistically significantly lower than 7.0 ($t(587) = -14.77, p < .001$).

---

## Two-Sample t-Test (Welch's Test): Testing RQ3

Comparing Semester 2 wellbeing across Workshop vs Control groups:

```r
workshop_test <- t.test(wellbeing ~ workshop, data = semester2)
workshop_test
```

```
	Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  wellbeing by workshop
t = 5.7629, df = 596.88, p-value = 1.391e-08
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Invited and group Not invited is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 3.435431 6.984569
sample estimates:
    mean in group Invited mean in group Not invited 
                 65.21000                  60.00000 
```

- **Welch's $t$-test** does not assume equal variances between groups.
- The 5.21 point gain is highly significant ($t(596.9) = 5.76, p < .001$).
- Because students were **randomly assigned**, we can state that the workshop **caused** this gain!

---

## Standardized Effect Size: Cohen's d

A 5.21-point difference on a 0–100 scale: is that large or small?

$$d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{\text{pooled}}} = \frac{65.21 - 60.00}{11.08} = 0.47$$

```r
inv <- semester2$wellbeing[semester2$workshop == "Invited"]
ctl <- semester2$wellbeing[semester2$workshop == "Not invited"]

d_val <- (mean(inv) - mean(ctl)) / sqrt((var(inv) + var(ctl)) / 2)
round(d_val, 2)
#> [1] 0.47
```

### Cohen's (1988) Effect Size Benchmarks:
- $d = 0.20$: Small
- $d = 0.50$: Medium
- $d = 0.80$: Large

The workshop produced a **moderate effect** ($d = 0.47$)—substantively meaningful for a 6-week brief intervention.

---

## Paired t-Test: Measuring Change Within Subjects

Did the **invited students themselves** improve between Semester 1 and Semester 2?

```r
library(tidyr)

invited_paired <- semesters |>
  filter(semester %in% c(1, 2)) |>
  left_join(students, join_by(student_id)) |>
  filter(workshop == "Invited") |>
  select(student_id, semester, wellbeing) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = semester, values_from = wellbeing, names_prefix = "sem_")

t.test(invited_paired$sem_2, invited_paired$sem_1, paired = TRUE)
```

```
	Paired t-test

data:  invited_paired$sem_2 and invited_paired$sem_1
t = 6.8421, df = 299, p-value = 3.912e-11
mean of the differences 
                   4.81 
```

- Paired tests eliminate between-person variance, increasing statistical power.
- **Methodological Warning:** The paired test alone cannot prove causality because it lacks a control group (students might simply feel better in Semester 2).

---

# Non-Parametric Rank Tests

### What to Do When Normality Assumptions Fail

---

## Mann-Whitney U Test (Wilcoxon Rank-Sum)

When data is ordinal or severely skewed with small $N$, compare **ranks** instead of raw values:

```r
# Testing skewed caffeine intake across genders:
wilcox.test(caffeine_mg ~ gender, data = first_sem)
```

```
	Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  caffeine_mg by gender
W = 44210, p-value = 0.4821
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
```

- Medians: Females = 230 mg, Males = 250 mg.
- $W = 44210, p = .482$ (no significant difference in caffeine intake ranks).

---

## Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test (Paired Non-Parametric)

The non-parametric counterpart to the paired $t$-test:

```r
wilcox.test(invited_paired$sem_2, invited_paired$sem_1, paired = TRUE)
```

```
	Wilcoxon signed rank test with continuity correction

data:  invited_paired$sem_2 and invited_paired$sem_1
V = 32840, p-value = 1.124e-10
```

Both parametric ($t = 6.84$) and non-parametric ($V = 32840$) tests reach the identical conclusion ($p < .001$).

---

# Categorical Inference: Chi-Square ($\chi^2$) Tests

### Comparing Observed Frequencies with Expected Frequencies

---

## Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test

Testing whether a single categorical variable matches expected population proportions (e.g., 50/50 gender balance):

$$\chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E}$$

```r
table(students$gender)
#> Female   Male 
#>    312    288 

chisq.test(table(students$gender), p = c(0.5, 0.5))
```

```
	Chi-squared test for given probabilities

data:  table(students$gender)
X-squared = 0.96, df = 1, p-value = 0.3272
```

$\chi^2(1) = 0.96, p = .327$. The sample does not deviate significantly from a 50/50 ratio.

---

## Chi-Square Test of Independence

Testing whether two categorical variables are associated:

```r
job_tab <- table(students$employment, students$considering_dropout)
job_tab
```

```
                No Yes
  None         276  42
  Part-time    119  21
  Full-time    107  35
```

```r
job_test <- chisq.test(job_tab)
job_test
```

```
	Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  job_tab
X-squared = 8.4121, df = 2, p-value = 0.01491
```

Employment and dropout thoughts are significantly associated ($\chi^2(2) = 8.41, p = .015$).

---

## Inspecting Expected Cell Counts

Chi-square tests require that all expected cell frequencies exceed $5$:

```r
round(job_test$expected, 1)
```

```
                  No  Yes
  None         266.1 51.9
  Part-time    117.1 22.9
  Full-time    118.8 23.2
```

All expected counts are $> 20$. If any expected count falls below 5, use **Fisher's Exact Test** (`fisher.test()`).

---

# Selecting the Right Statistical Test

### The Master Inference Decision Tree

---

## Inference Decision Matrix

```
                      WHAT IS THE OUTCOME VARIABLE?
                                    |
          +-------------------------+-------------------------+
          |                                                   |
      NUMERIC                                            CATEGORICAL
          |                                                   |
How many groups to compare?                       How many categorical variables?
  - 1 Group vs Mu  ==> One-Sample t-test            - 1 Variable ==> Chi-Square Goodness of Fit
  - 2 Independent  ==> Two-Sample t-test (Welch)    - 2 Variables==> Chi-Square Independence
  - 2 Paired/PrePost=> Paired t-test
  - 3+ Groups      ==> One-Way ANOVA (Chapter 8)
  
  [If severely skewed + small N]:
  - 2 Independent  ==> Mann-Whitney U test
  - 2 Paired       ==> Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test
```

---

# Writing APA Results Sections

### Communicating Statistical Evidence with Rigour

---

## Reporting Guidelines for Statistical Results

### Four Rules for Thesis Writing:
1. **Never Report a $p$-Value Alone:** Always state means, SDs, and confidence intervals.
2. **Report Exact $p$-Values:** Write $p = .015$ or $p = .048$; reserve $p < .001$ for extremely small numbers.
3. **Include Effect Sizes:** Always accompany $t$-tests with Cohen's $d$.
4. **Link Back to the Substantive Hypothesis:** State clearly whether $H_0$ was rejected.

---

## Publication-Ready Thesis Examples

### One-Sample t-Test:
> "Graduate students reported sleeping significantly fewer hours than the recommended 7.0-hour threshold ($M = 6.38$, $SD = 1.02$), $t(587) = -14.77$, $p < .001$, $95\%\text{ CI } [6.30, 6.46]$."

### Two-Sample t-Test:
> "Students randomly assigned to the wellbeing workshop demonstrated significantly higher wellbeing at the conclusion of Semester 2 ($M = 65.21$, $SD = 10.95$) than uninvited control participants ($M = 60.00$, $SD = 11.20$), representing a moderate intervention effect, $t(596.9) = 5.76$, $p < .001$, $d = 0.47$, $95\%\text{ CI } [3.44, 6.98]$. The null hypothesis was rejected."

### Chi-Square Test:
> "Thoughts of program dropout differed significantly by employment status, $\chi^2(2, N = 600) = 8.41$, $p = .015$. Students holding full-time jobs exhibited the highest prevalence of considering dropout ($24.6\%$), compared to $15.0\%$ of part-time workers and $13.2\%$ of non-employed peers."

---

## Statistical Inference Checklist

Before finalizing your thesis results chapter:

- [ ] **Data Independence Checked:** Observations represent distinct participants (or accounted for via paired design).
- [ ] **Two-Tailed Standard:** Used conservative two-tailed tests unless strictly justified a priori.
- [ ] **Welch Default:** Used Welch's two-sample test (did not assume equal variances).
- [ ] **Effect Sizes Calculated:** Cohen's $d$ reported alongside all significant $t$-tests.
- [ ] **Assumption Violations Addressed:** Non-parametric tests deployed for ordinal/severely skewed small datasets.
- [ ] **Expected Cell Counts Verified:** Confirmed all expected cells $\ge 5$ before reporting $\chi^2$.
- [ ] **No Causal Overreach:** Causal language restricted strictly to randomized experimental manipulations.

---

## Summary of Core R Inference Functions

| Test | Function | Example |
|---|---|---|
| One-sample t-test | `t.test()` | `t.test(x, mu = 7)` |
| Two-sample t-test | `t.test()` | `t.test(y ~ group, data = df)` |
| Paired t-test | `t.test()` | `t.test(post, pre, paired = TRUE)` |
| Mann-Whitney U | `wilcox.test()` | `wilcox.test(y ~ group, data = df)` |
| Wilcoxon Signed-Rank | `wilcox.test()` | `wilcox.test(post, pre, paired = TRUE)` |
| Chi-square Goodness of Fit | `chisq.test()` | `chisq.test(table(x), p = c(0.5, 0.5))` |
| Chi-square Independence | `chisq.test()` | `chisq.test(table(x, y))` |
| Power calculation | `power.t.test()` | `power.t.test(n = 300, delta = 5, sd = 11)` |
